title: What is TREPS in mutual funds, and why does your fund hold it?
summary: TREPS is tri-party repo: short-term lending of a fund's spare cash against government securities via CCIL. Learn how it works and how safe it is.
body_markdown:
TREPS stands for tri-party repo. When your mutual fund shows a TREPS line, it has lent spare cash for a short time against government securities. The deal runs through a system of the Clearing Corporation of India (CCIL). TREPS is not a company or a share, and you cannot buy it yourself.


A mutual fund is a pool of money from many people, invested by a professional manager under SEBI rules.


## What is TREPS in mutual funds?


TREPS is a short loan of cash, backed by government securities, arranged through CCIL. A government security, or G-sec, is a loan to the government. Collateral is the asset a borrower hands over to the lender as safety for the loan.


The word "repo" is short for repurchase. RBI describes a repo as borrowing money by selling securities. The seller agrees to buy them back on a set future date at an agreed price. That price includes interest for the money borrowed.


"Tri-party" means a third entity sits between the borrower and the lender. In RBI's definition, this tri-party agent helps with collateral selection, payment and settlement, custody and management while the deal lasts. In TREPS that third party is CCIL, which also acts as the central counterparty to every trade. Put plainly, it stands in the middle of each deal.


Some facts about the deals themselves, from CCIL's own material:


- Borrowing and lending is offered for terms of up to the next 7 days, plus the next three month-ends. A member can ask for another term of up to 365 days.
- The minimum amount, and each step above it, is ₹5 lakh.
- The collateral is government securities and treasury bills. CCIL publishes a list of securities that qualify.


A treasury bill, or T-bill, is a short-term loan to the government for 91, 182 or 364 days. TREPS has been in use since November 2018. A fund house's notice from that month records it replacing an older system called CBLO.


## How does a TREPS deal work?


In a TREPS deal, one side lends cash, the other borrows it, and CCIL handles the collateral between them.


The parties:


- **Borrower:** receives the cash and gives government securities as collateral.
- **Lender:** hands over the cash. A mutual fund is often on this side, because it has spare cash to put to work.
- **CCIL:** matches the two, moves the collateral and cash, and collects margin. Margin is money members deposit with CCIL to cover the risk of loss on their trades.


Under CCIL's rules, securities covering the amount borrowed move into the lender's account with CCIL. They stay there until the loan is repaid.


Here is a simple illustration, using arithmetic on a past day's rate. Say a fund lends ₹200 crore for one night. On 30 September 2026, CCIL recorded an average TREPS rate of 5.0735% a year for its most liquid term. At that rate, one night's interest comes to about ₹2,78,000. That is roughly ₹14 a night on every ₹1 lakh lent.


The next morning the cash is back with the fund, ready for redemptions or another night's lending. Redemption means you sell your units back to the fund and get the money. The rate changes every day, so this is a picture of one day, not a promise of anything.


## Why does a mutual fund hold TREPS?


A fund holds TREPS to keep cash earning something while it waits for its next use. SEBI does not require this, but its rules make TREPS convenient.


- **Pay redemptions on time.** SEBI's rule is that redemption proceeds reach the investor within 3 working days.
- **Avoid leaning on borrowing.** A fund may borrow only to meet temporary cash needs. Even then, it may borrow at most 20% of its net assets, meaning what it holds less what it owes, for up to six months.
- **Wait between investments.** Money that has come in but is not yet invested has to sit somewhere.


NFO money is one case. Before a new fund offer closes, SEBI lets the fund house park the money in triparty repo on government securities or treasury bills. No management fee is charged on it, and any gain on it must be passed on to investors. Our guide to[what an NFO is](https://koshex.com/blog/what-is-an-nfo) covers the offer itself.


Equity schemes may put the part not held in shares into money market and other liquid instruments. The money market means borrowing and lending for up to a year. So an equity fund may well have a small cash slice, and some of it can sit in TREPS.


Debt funds lend money by buying bonds and similar paper from governments, banks or companies. Three debt fund categories have short limits on what they hold. An[overnight fund](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/overnight-funds) invests in securities that mature in 1 day. A[liquid fund](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/liquid-funds) holds securities of up to 91 days, and a[money market fund](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/money-market-funds) up to 1 year.


## Is TREPS safe?


TREPS is low risk, not zero risk.


SEBI treats exposure to TREPS on G-secs or T-bills as exposure to government securities. So it stays outside the limit on lending to a single issuer, meaning one borrower, and outside the 20% sector limit. In SEBI's credit risk scoring, TREPS gets the top value of 13, the same as G-secs and cash. Each fund also carries a riskometer, SEBI's label that runs from Low to Very High. TREPS, G-secs and cash all score at the lowest-risk end of the debt parameters on it.


CCIL's controls work like this:


- Members deposit initial margin in advance, before they place any borrow or lend order.
- A borrower's limit is the value of its collateral net of a haircut, a deduction from the collateral's value.
- Collateral is revalued once the trading day closes, and several times during it.
- Margin for price moves is collected on trades that are still open.
- CCIL keeps a separate default fund for TREPS, to meet losses if a member fails to pay.


RBI says government securities carry practically no risk of default. It also lists other risks they do have, such as market, reinvestment and liquidity risk.


## TREPS vs repo, reverse repo, CBLO and treasury bills


TREPS is a repo with CCIL in the middle; repo, reverse repo, CBLO and treasury bills are related but different.


Term What it is


Repo Borrowing cash by selling securities and agreeing to buy them back with interest


Reverse repo The same deal seen from the lender's side


CBLO The older CCIL system for borrowing and lending, which TREPS replaced in November 2018


Treasury bill A loan to the government for 91, 182 or 364 days, issued by the Government of India at a discount and repaid at its full value


A treasury bill is the government borrowing, while TREPS is lending between market players with government securities as backup. Our article on[treasury bills](https://koshex.com/blog/treasury-bills) explains them in full.


The RBI repo rate is another separate thing. It is the rate at which RBI itself provides money under its liquidity facility. TREPS rates are set between market participants each day. RBI's 2025 repo Master Direction sets the rules for market repos.


For the dated comparison, the RBI's repo rate was 5.25% on 30 September 2026. The TREPS average that day was about 5.07%. To see how a change in interest rates can change the value of the bonds a debt fund holds, read[how interest rates affect mutual funds](https://koshex.com/blog/how-interest-rates-affect-mutual-funds) .


## Does SEBI make funds hold TREPS?


No. SEBI does not set a minimum share of a fund that must go into TREPS. Neither SEBI's master circular for mutual funds nor its mutual fund regulations sets a fixed percentage of liquid assets for TREPS.


What SEBI does is treat TREPS like government securities. It does not count toward the limits on lending to one company or one sector, and it scores as low risk. That makes it the natural place to park cash.


TREPS pays the short-term rate the market sets each day, and that interest is part of what the fund earns. A fund has a NAV, the price of one unit, not a share price that TREPS could drive up. For what NAV does and does not tell you, see[how important NAV is](https://koshex.com/blog/how-important-is-nav-when-choosing-mutual-funds) .


## How to read the TREPS line in your fund's factsheet


Look in the full monthly portfolio for a line called "TREPS" or "Triparty Repo". It is often grouped under cash.


In an overnight fund, lending of this kind can make up almost the whole portfolio. One overnight fund's factsheet for 31 August 2026 showed repo at 97.42% and triparty repo at 1.49%. The rest was in treasury bills and current assets.


In an equity fund, the TREPS line is part of the cash slice, kept until it is invested or paid out. Koshex reviews your holdings over time and flags changes, such as a fund's category, risk or ranking shifting.
